# Norn test vectors

This directory is the **cross-implementation contract** (`SPEC.md` §12). A
second implementation that reproduces everything here agrees with Norn on every
byte that matters, and one that does not has found either a bug or a hole in
the specification — both of which are worth knowing.

Nothing here needs this repository. The files are plain CBOR, JSON, text and
`tlog-tiles` directories, and `SPEC.md` beside them is the only document *of
this project* required to interpret any of it.

It is not self-contained, and says so: §16.2 states plainly that "a reader who
does not fetch BIP-350 cannot implement this section", and §8.1 and §11.1 defer
their proof algorithms to RFC 6962 rather than restating them. The preamble
lists every such dependency. `SPEC.md` tells you what Norn decides; the
standards it names tell you what it reuses.

## Provenance — four, stated plainly

A vector proves a format, not a fact about the world, and how much it proves
depends on who wrote the bytes.

| Produced by | What | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| **`contrib/norn-ref`** (the Python reference) | entries, state, trust, enrollment requests | Written from `SPEC.md` by a second implementation; the Go code must match them, not the other way round |
| **`cmd/norn-genlog`** (this project's Go) | `replayed-policy/`, `quorum-none/`, `genesis-unapplied/`, `heads-run16/`, the `receipt-bad/` extension, `served/`, `served-large/`, `grown-log/`, `proofs/`, `fork/`, `checkpoints-good/`, `checkpoints-bad/` | Producing a tiled log requires a log. Validated against libraries neither implementation wrote: `transparency-dev/formats` parses the checkpoint and `x/mod/sumdb/tlog` checks every inclusion proof |
| **`python-opentimestamps`** (the OTS reference) | `anchors/` | Norn reads `.ots` files and never writes them, so the suite's copies come from the implementation that owns the format |
| **C2SP/CCTV** (upstream Ed25519 set) | `ed25519-cctv/` | 914 independent edge vectors, kept byte for byte with their BSD-3-Clause license and digest provenance; Norn derives only the outcome table |

Regenerate the first two with `make vectors` and `make vectors-log`. The third
is never regenerated — see `contrib/ots-vector/`, and the reason is the point
of having it.

## Layout

| Path | What it is |
|---|---|
| `ed25519-cctv/` | §3.1's 914 C2SP CCTV Ed25519 vectors: untouched upstream JSON, README and license, with `PROVENANCE.md`; `gen_cases.py` derives `cases.json` for NORN-ED25519-v1 (913 rejects by first deciding flag, vector 305 accepts), not RFC 8032 |
| `keys.json` | every test key: Ed25519 `{seed, public, kid}` by name, X25519 public keys, and `net` |
| `entries/` | one valid entry per type, canonical bytes, each with a `.json` mirror carrying its hashes and preimage |
| `log/` | the 162-entry replay fixture. **Read the order from `manifest.json`**, never by sorting filenames; entries that must be refused carry a `.reason` file. `51-enroll-unicode-labels` is accepted with malformed reserved hints and preserves them in `state.json`. `133-bad-root_add-counts-its-own-key` is the §4.2 case: a `root_add` signed by two of three roots and by the key in its own body, which is `threshold` because signatures resolve against the state BEFORE the entry |
| `state.json` | the state those 162 entries replay to, in canonical JSON (§14) |
| `proven/grant-labels.json` | 49 pure-function `{label, grant, says}` cases with a `comment`: router masking, badgrant whole-label failure, an IPv4-mapped prefix giving no grant, the RFC 5952 first-run tie-break and duplicates removed after masking; run 17 D11 adds text order across address families and refusal of eight groups beside `::`; run 18 accepts seven explicit groups with `::` consuming exactly one; run 19 adds `10.0.0.0/8,  fd00::/64`, `  10.0.0.0/8  ` and `::1.2.3.4/128`, pinning every surrounding space and the compatible address rendered as `::102:304/128`. Run 20 adds the hexadecimal mapped spellings `::ffff:a00:1/128` and `0:0:0:0:0:ffff:a00:1/128`, each no grant. |
| `proven/` | the devices a node admits at four evaluation times, including the boundary where `expires == T`, and under `grants` each active device's §4.0 grant (D-073). `state.json` is clock-independent on purpose, and `quorum-none/` exercises expiry without a quorum time — the rule that decides when a device stops being admitted |
| `entries-hostile/` | 17 inputs at the profile boundaries: the nine `bare-` cases are one banned item each — null, undefined, float, simple value 16, negative integer, tag, indefinite length, a non-text map key and an invalid UTF-8 string — with no schema above them, so only the profile can refuse. The rest are input at and past §4.0's three resource limits — the entry size, the nesting depth and the map-key cap. A case with `says` must be refused for that reason; one marked `accepted` sits exactly at a limit and must be accepted, which is what bounds the limit from below |
| `entries-utf8/` | `bare-surrogate.cbor` is exactly `63eda080`, invalid UTF-8; changing only its text to U+E000 (`63ee8080`) decodes; `cases.json` gives its §4.0 rule |
| `genesis/` | twenty-seven ways a genesis entry is refused. `18` and `19` are step 7's two halves — the **role** a signature declares and the **key set** it resolves against; `20` is a `name` one byte past the 64-byte cap; `21` and `22` give a threshold as the boolean `true`, which a reader that coerces it to 1 accepts (SEC-016). `23-root-order-eight` and `24-root-noncanonical` append an invalid key to the three honest roots and retain two honest root signatures, so only §3.1 aborts them as `bad-genesis`; `27-type-with-genesis-body` carries a genuine genesis body under t = note, with a valid root quorum and its own leaf pin, so only the type rule aborts it |
| `genesis-good/` | geneses a reader MUST accept, one single-entry log each with the state it replays to: `01-name-at-the-cap`, a `name` of exactly 64 bytes in two-byte characters, and `02-name-one-byte`, the one-byte floor (§4.0). The other side of `genesis/`'s name bound |
| `trust.cbor`, `trust.toml`, `trust.fingerprint` | the anchor in both encodings, and the fingerprint an operator compares out of band (§9.3) |
| `log-empty/` | a log with no entries at all, and the zero state §5.1 says it replays to. A reader that treats no genesis as a missing one reports `bad-genesis` instead |
| `log-admission/` | a separate nine-entry log using the same manifest/state contract: fixture genesis, `01-signer_add-mixed-order`, `02-root_add-mixed-order` and `03-log_key-mixed-order` (all root-signed, all `decode`), admitted `04-signer_add-honest` and `05-enroll-honest`, `06-rotate-mixed-order` (signed by the current device key and cofactored-validly by the incoming key, `decode`), root-signed `07-policy-small-order` (order-8 witness key, `decode`), and admitted `08-policy-honest`. `state.json` records exactly five refusals, the honest signer and device additions, and the final honest policy; `log/` and its served state are unchanged |
| `log-edges/` | a separate 15-entry replay log for runs 14 and 18: whole-string IDs, inclusive integer and reason bounds, re-enrolment label replacement, body-before-lookup order, request point admission and distinct witness algorithm; run 18 adds root-signed `13-policy-log-cosignature-key.cbor`, a current-prev policy with a distinct valid 0x04 log key (`decode`), repaired only by its algorithm and derived id plus envelope signatures; its own four-member anchor, `entries`, `codes`, `rules`, `state.json` and `.reason` files. Run 19 adds accepted `14-enroll-c1-label.cbor`: a fresh device with `labels.note` equal to `next<U+0085>line`; `state.json` emits C2 85 verbatim, never a backslash-u escape. |
| `log-republish/` | D-078 and run 16 in 18 entries, with its own anchor, manifest, codes, rules, state and ten refusal reasons: a stripped revoke is `threshold` and its genuine entry revokes nas; a note preimage is `decode` and its signed note accepts; copies of applied content and refused bytes are `dup-entry`; anchor and learned log keys are `dup-key`, a new key accepts; a root-signed policy naming zürich is `decode`, zurich accepts. `13-params-two-byte-true` is `decode`; `14-params-canonical-true` changes only `f8 15` to `f5` and accepts, setting `rotate_needs_signer` true. `15-copy-genesis-extra-sig` preserves genesis content under one extra sorted unresolvable signature and is `dup-entry`. `16-policy-text-at-the-cap` accepts a parseable 4096-byte policy; `17-policy-text-one-past-the-cap` is `decode` at 4097 bytes. Both use two-byte comment padding |
| `log-rules/` | 45 entries for runs 16 L8, 17 D11, 18 L1–L2 and D-080 (1), with its own four-member anchor, manifest, codes, rules, state and twenty refusal reasons. Another device cannot revoke nas; governance prev is mandatory even at zero; ts is mandatory; an empty label value accepts; a policy log line may pre-announce a log key. Reordered signatures on an applied enrollment give decode before content duplication; root removal checks unknown-key before root-invariant. The main log remains 162 entries. Each dual fault is repaired separately and together against its own prefix, exposing both codes and then accepting. Run 20 appends `40-log-key-point-before-prev` and `41-log-key-point-repaired-stale-prev`, a 32-byte order-8 point beside its point-only repair, both with stale prev (`decode`, then `stale-state`). |
| `log-cas/` | 33 entries and 17 refusals for D-077: five stale withheld-authorisation stories, predecessor presence, the log/witness public-key invariant, five precedence cases, and an accepted rotation with one signature when the incoming device key is the current key. | `trust-good/` | twelve trust files §9.1 **permits**: a witness with no `url`, an `anchor` whose `type` this version does not know, opaque and mismatched URL strings, a present empty witness URL, and `at-the-cap`, exactly `MAX_TRUST_BYTES` long (`trust-bad/41-one-past-the-cap` is the same file one byte longer). `policy-over-4096.cbor` changes only the policy text of `trust.cbor`, growing it to 4097 bytes with one ignored comment line while the whole file stays below `MAX_TRUST_BYTES`; `cases.json` gives its `says` and §9.1 rule. | `trust-bad/` | 58 anchors that must be rejected. `07` and `08` isolate the no-witness and duplicate-name rules; `13`, `42` and `43` isolate derived-origin equality, witness-key correspondence and the closed-anchor rule. `40` is the log-key name plus one character, so only equality refuses it. `37` and `39` change one declared key ID, in the log key and a witness key, and carry that key into the policy too so only recomputation refuses them. `44-log-key-base64-cr` leaves the key bytes unchanged and is refused because its base64 data contains a carriage return. `45-origin-case-changed` changes one letter of `origin` to uppercase and renames the log key, in the file and its policy, to agree; only the exact derivation of `origin` from `net` refuses it. `46-log-key-name-case-changed` keeps `origin` honest and changes one letter's case in the log key's name, so only exact name equality refuses it. `47-witness-noncanonical-point` uses the negative-zero x encoding in a witness verifier key and carries the same key into the policy, so only §3.1 invalidates the anchor. `54-witness-name-not-ascii` names zürich in both the witness array and policy and is invalid. `56-policy-log-key-renamed` keeps the log public key under another policy verifier name; `57-log-url-bytes`, `58-anchor-max-lag-text` and `59-witness-url-uint` each break one §9.1 member type. | `receipt-good/` | two receipts that MUST be accepted: `deadline-at-the-cap.note`, deadline 9223372036854775807, and `deadline-zero-no-clock.note`, deadline 0, each bound to the genesis leaf. `cases.json` supplies `now: 0`, the `accept` code and §7 rule; a different submitted leaf is still `entry`. The zero deadline expires at a nonzero checking time and accepts again with only the checking time returned to zero |
| `policies/` | SPEC §9.1's C2SP `tlog-policy` grammar: 71 cases, 18 accepted and 53 refused. `cases.json` says which whole policies MUST parse or MUST be refused, and why; `evaluate` tables pin what each quorum means. `all-members.txt` requires both pi and vps, with either singleton refused and both accepted. `bad-log-vkey-algorithm-distinct.txt` isolates a valid 0x04 log key without a duplicate public key; changing only its algorithm and derived id to 0x01 repairs it. `trailing-space.txt` and `trailing-tab.txt` append two spaces or one tab to every directive, including the log, every witness and quorum; both parse exactly like the space-free policy, and each carries `says` and a rule citing §9.1's trailing-whitespace row. The files are byte-exact: every line, including a final comment, needs a line feed. `bad-final-comment-no-lf` is the minimal policy followed by `# note` without LF, refused solely for that missing delimiter (D-076). `directive-after-quorum` accepts an unused witness and group after the quorum; all four cosigner sets decide identically with those lines removed. `bad-redefinition-after-use` refuses only the later redefinition of a group the quorum already used; removing that line parses. Cases cover quorum ordering, reserved names, verifier-key IDs and algorithms, duplicate public keys across vkey aliases and directive types, threshold bounds, CRLF, and forbidden ASCII controls (including controls hidden inside comments). Non-ASCII whitespace such as U+00A0 and U+0085 remains content. `two-log-lines` is accepted because its keys differ; the aliases are refused because their underlying public keys match. The extra-final-newline note-framing case cannot be re-signed, and the expired cases give their checking time explicitly. Binding decodes structure, field rules and points; it does not check the request signature or network. Run 18 adds `index-outside-tree.bundle`, index 1 of a one-leaf tree with an empty proof (`inclusion`); changing only the index to 0 accepts. `padded-proof` appends one 32-byte hash to `proofs/nas.bundle` and is `inclusion`; `one-past-the-cap` is the positive cap bundle grown by one byte to 81920, otherwise sound and refused as `bundle` on length; a wrong entry, a foreign checkpoint, a tampered proof, a checkpoint signed by a key the anchor does not name, one with no witness quorum and one whose checkpoint names another origin. `cases.json` gives the log key, what each refusal must be about, and in `codes` the SPEC §10.1 code each MUST be refused with. Run 17 adds `short-proof-hash` (`bundle`), `request-device-pk-small-order` and `pk-length-under-own-id` (`binding`), each beside a sound bundle. |
| `served-genesis/` | §10.1's `genesis`, for a reader that holds **no** checkpoint: `cases.json` serves `../detect/other-genesis` (this network's log key, origin and witnesses over a history whose entry 0 is not the anchored genesis) and `../detect/empty` (a cosigned head over no entries), each refused `genesis`. `detect/` serves the same two to a reader that holds a head, which answers `fork` and `rollback`. `other-genesis-missing-tile` and `other-genesis-tampered-tile` serve the matching new directories in `detect/`: `genesis` precedes the missing or tampered tile, with no held head. |
| `detect/` | **pairs**, not single artifacts: a checkpoint the reader already holds and one it is then offered, each branch served with its own tiles. These six are built to fail more than one step, and are coded with the earliest (others fail more than one incidentally — `bad-open-schema` and `bad-wrong-version` are built on `bad-consistent`): `bad-oversize-and-not-cbor` is `oversize` and not `cbor`, because the size bound is checked before any parse; `bad-other-origin`, wrong in both checkpoints, is `held` and not `conflicting`; `bad-version-and-unknown-key` is `version` and not `schema`, because a key set is only closed relative to a version; `bad-short-held-root-and-size-above-held` is `schema` and not `size`, because a hash's length is part of the schema; `bad-policy-unparseable-and-foreign-held` is `policy` and not `held`, because the unparseable carried policy is step 4 and the foreign held checkpoint is step 5. Version 2 adds `bad-split-above-size`, `bad-split-proof-held`, `bad-split-proof-conflicting` and `bad-split-zero-with-a-proof` (`proof`), `bad-split-root-length` and `bad-twelve-keys` (`schema`), and `bad-version-three` (`version`). `cases.json`'s `sound` names eleven files that MUST prove a fork: the five version-2 originals, `evidence`, `policy-not-the-readers`, `evidence-at-64`, `evidence-at-the-cap` (exactly `MAX_EVIDENCE_BYTES` long), and `evidence-at-same-size`, each retained as `<name>-v1.cbor` too (proves the fork, claims no split), and `evidence-understated-split` (split 39 rather than 40, with valid proofs to both heads, accepted because §11.1 permits understating). `evidence-at-64` is at a power-of-two size below the held one, the consistency-proof shape RFC 6962 handles with its own branch. `evidence-at-same-size` holds `served/checkpoint` and a conflicting head of the same size with a different root, signed by the log key and cosigned by all three witnesses; its proof is empty and `held_root` is held's signed root. `policy-not-the-readers.cbor` is the positive twin: a carried policy the reader does not share, which MUST still prove the fork. The original `fork/evidence.cbor` and `proofs/nas.bundle` accept for either reader |
| `quorum-none/` | Go-generated trust differing only in its `quorum none` policy, and the served head with all witness lines removed. `cases.json` accepts that head and `../served/checkpoint` over served tiles and gives the proven set for each, including contractor: no quorum time means expiry cannot be judged, even with valid witness lines |
| `genesis-unapplied/` | Go-generated one-entry tiled log, log-signed and cosigned to quorum, with a trust file pinning that exact entry's leaf hash. Removing one of the fixture genesis's two root signatures prevents it applying: `genesis`. `cases.json` pairs it with `sound/`, restoring the signature and original trust, which accepts. A reader checking only the leaf hash accepts an empty set |
| `heads-run16/` | six Go-generated heads over `served/`'s honest tiles, with their own `trust.cbor`, `codes` and one-raw-line `rules` in `cases.json`: three accepted strangers, a three-byte payload (`note`), a policy-only log signer (`log-signature`) after replaying `00-genesis.cbor` and root-signed `01-policy-logkey3.cbor` (prev 0), and a forged pi line beside a short quorum (`cosignature`). The separate `requests` table carries `consumer_net` and two Go-generated signed requests, one accepted and one refused for another network; these semantic results have no closed refusal code (§16.1) |
| `anchors/` | OpenTimestamps proofs, and a calendar's reply, written by `python-opentimestamps`. **Start at `cases.json`**: it gives each proof's digest in hex and names the bytes that produce it, so you can check the rule without parsing the OpenTimestamps container — a format `SPEC.md` does not describe. The checkpoint proof is over `served/checkpoint` **through the newline that terminates the blank separator line** — the three body lines plus the blank line, four `0x0A`. That is not the three-line body and not §7's signed text; anchoring is advisory, so a reader that picks the wrong one of the three never matches a stamp and never says so |

## `SHA256SUMS`

For somebody who downloaded this directory and does not have the generators:
`shasum -a 256 -c SHA256SUMS` from inside it says whether the set is whole and
unmodified. Regenerate with `make vectors-sums` after any change; a test fails
if it is stale.

## Using them

Start at `keys.json` and `entries/`: they need no network, no log and no
crypto beyond Ed25519 and SHA-256. Then `log/manifest.json` and `state.json`,
which together are §5's replay in one comparison. `served/` and `proofs/` need
a `tlog-tiles` reader. `trust-bad/`, `requests-bad/` and `log/*.reason` are the
half most implementations get wrong: each is a file that **must be refused**,
and for the stated reason.

**`cases.json`'''s `says` field is a semantic hint**, not the bytes your
implementation must produce. §5.2, §7, §10.1 and §11.1 each give their layer a
closed list of codes, and a manifest's `codes` map is what to compare against
(§12); `says` is for the rules that have none: map each onto your own error by
hand, once. What it is for is the discipline it
enforces here — a negative must be refused for its own rule and nothing else,
and a phrase naming that rule is how the generators check it.

A file being absent from this list is a bug in the list — a test in
`internal/specdoc` fails if anything here is undescribed.
